Judgment:
1. The present is a complaint filed under section 16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954
(herein after referred to as Pfa Act), alleging that the accused have violated the provisions of t
he PFA Act and Rules.
DA vs Bal Kishan & Ors.

2. As per the complaint, on 31.07.2002, the Food Inspector (herein after referred as FI) Sh Bal Mukand purchased a sample of 'Moong Dal (Dhuli)" a food article for analysis from accused Bal Kishan at M/s Purna Giri General Store, Shop No. 4, Krishna Menon Lane, New Delhi -11, where the said food article was found stored for sale and where accused No.1 Bal Kishan was found conducting the business of the said food article at the time of sampling.
The sample consisted 600 grams of Da vs Bal Kishan & Ors.

1 Moong Dal(Dhuli) taken from an open gunny bag bearing no label declaration.
The sample was taken under the supervision / direction of Sh. S.M. Haider, SDM/LHA.
The sample was taken after proper homogenization with the help of clean and dry jhaba by rotating in all possible directions.
The Food Inspector divided the sample then and there into three equal parts by putting into three clean and dry bottles.
Each bottle was separately packed, fastened and sealed according to PFA Act and Rules.
The vendor's signatures were obtained on the LHA slip and the wrapper of the sample bottles.
Notice was given to accused No. 1 Bal Kishan and the price of sample was also given to him vide vendor receipt dated 31.07.2002.
Panchnama too was prepared at the spot.
All the documents prepared by F.I. were signed by accused No.1 Bal Kishan and the other witness Sh Jeet Ram, FI,

Before starting sample proceeding efforts were made to join public witnesses but none came forward, as such FI Sh Jeet Ram was joined as witness.
3.
One counter-part of the sample bearing LHA code No. SMH/LHA/004772 was also sent to Public Analyst, Delhi in intact DA vs Bal Kishan & Ors.
condition and two counter-parts were deposited with the LHA in intact condition.
Public Analyst analysed the sample and found the same to be adulterated.

The report of the Public Analyst is as follows:
"The sample is adulterated because it is coloured with synthetic colouring matter viz tartarzine."
4.
It is the case of the complainant that accused No.1 Bal Kishan was the vendor-cum-proprietor of M/s Purna Giri General Store, Shop No. 4, Krishna Menon Lane, New Delhi -11 at the time of sampling.

The vendor disclosed that the sample commodity was purchased from accused No. 2 Mukesh Kumar M/s Shyam Lal Raj Kumar, 4053/55, Naya Bazar, Delhi - 6 as such both the vendor and proprietor of supplier firm are being prosecuted.
5.
Thereafter on completion of investigation, sanction under section 20 of the PFA Act was obtained from the Director PFA.

The complaint was then filed in the court on 02.04.2003 alleging violation of section 2(ia)(j)&(m) of PFA Act, 1954 and Rule 23 read with Rule 28 & 29 of PFA Rules, 1955 as punishable section 7/16(1)(a) of PFA Act against the accused.
6. As the complaint was filed in writing by a public servant, recording of pre-summoning evidence was dispensed with and the accused were summoned vide order dated 02.04.2003.
The accused thereafter exercised their option of analysing the counter part through CFL under section 13 (2) of the PFA Act.
Based on the report of the CFL as well as evidence led in pre charge evidence, charge was framed against the accused for commission of the DA vs Bal Kishan & Ors.

offence punishable under section 7/16(1) (A) PFA Act being violation of Section 2(ia)(a)(b)(j)&(m)
and Rule 23 read with Rule 28 & 29 of PFA Rules, 1955, to which accused pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.
Da vs Bal Kishan & Ors.

2 7.
At the trial, the prosecution examined three witness in support of its case i.e. PW-1 SDM/LHA Sh S.M. Haider, PW-2 FI Bal Mukand and PW-3 FI Jeet Ram.

PW-2 and PW-3 were part of the team that had visited the spot for sample proceedings under the supervision of SDM/LHA Sh.S.M.
Haider.

These witness narrated the steps undertaken by them during the sample proceedings,
including disclosing their identity, expressing intention to purchase sample for analysis, lifting the sample commodity of 600 grams of "Moong Dal(Dhuli)" from the vendor for analysis which was lying in an open gunny bag, bearing no label declaration, dividing the sample into three equal parts by putting them into three clean and dry glass bottles, separately sealing, packing and marking the same and obtaining signatures of vendor and witnesses.
They also proved the necessary documents including the vendor's receipt Ex.PW-1/A, Notice Ex. PW-1/B, Panchnama Ex.PW-1/C.
The vendor gave his statement Ex.PW1/D and also furnished photocopy of bill Mark A.

Thereafter, on 01.08.2002 one counterpart of the sample along with one copy of memo in form VII and another copy of memo in form VII in sealed deposited with PA vide receipt Ex.PW1/F and the remaining two counter parts of the sample in intact condition along with two copies of memo of Form VII in a sealed packet were deposited with LHA vide LHA Receipt Ex.PW1/E under intimation that one counterpart of the same has already been deposited with PA.
Thereafter, PA Report DA vs Bal Kishan & Ors.

sentences.text: Ex.PW1/G was received, according to which the sample was adulterated because it is coloured with synthetic colouring matter vix tartrazine.

Thereafter PW-2 FI Bal Mukand further investigated the matter and sent letter Ex.PW2/A to STO, Ward No. 99 and received its reply stating that accused Bal Kishan was the proprietor of M/s Purna Giri Genral Store.

PW-2 also received letter Ex.PW2/B from the accused Bal Kishan alongwith documents Mark B & C. PW-2 FI Bal Mukand also received a reply vide Ex.PW2/D from STO Ward No. 29 stating that accused Mukesh Kumar was the Proprietor of M/s Shyam Lal Raj Kumar.
Notice under section 14 A Ex.PW2/E addressed to Shyam Lal Raj Kumar was also prepared at the spot.
After completion of investigation, the entire case file was put before then Director PFA for obtaining his Consent.
The then Director PFA granted his Consent for prosecution vide sanction order Ex.PW1/H.
Thereafter, the present complaint Ex.PW1/J was filed before the Court.
Then intimation letter Ex.PW1/K alongwith copy of PA Reports was sent to the accused vide postal receipt Ex.PW1/L which was received back undelivered.
These witnesses were duly cross-examined by Ld. Defence Counsel.
8. Statement of the accused under section 313 CrPC were recorded on 02.08.2013 wherein the accused persons denied the allegations and pleaded innocence.
Thereafter matter was listed for defence evidence.
9. In defence, the accused No. 2 Mukesh Kumar examined himself as DW-1 and placed on record challan Ex.DW1/A and copy of bill Ex.DW1/B.

The accused No. 1 Bal Kishan also examined himself DA vs Bal Kishan & Ors.
as DW-2.
Thereafter defence evidence was closed vide order dated 29.07.2016 and the matter was fixed for final arguments.
Da vs Bal Kishan & Ors.

3 10.
In a criminal case, the burden is on the prosecution to prove its case against the accused beyond reasonable doubt by leading positive evidence.
This burden cannot be shifted to the accused and it has to be necessary discharged by the prosecution itself.

11.It is to be understood that the charge framed against the accused is for violation of section 2(ia)(a)(b), (j) and (m) of the PFA Act read with Rules 23 and 29 of PFA Rules with respect to 'adulteration'.

Under section 2(ia)(a) of PFA Act, the prosecution has to establish that the purchaser had demanded a food article of a specific nature, substance or quality and the article sold was, to his prejudice, either not of the nature, substance or quality demanded, or was not of the nature,
substance or quality which it purported or represented to be.
Section 2(ia)(j) specifically deals with colouring matter which is present other than prescribed or is present beyond the prescribed limits of variability.

Section 2(ia)
(m) of PFA Act deals with situation where the quality or purity of an article falls below the prescribed standard or its constituents are present in quantities not within the prescribed limits of variability.
12. The commodity in the present case is Dal Arhar which is food grain and has to be tested as per the standards prescribed for food grains.
It is clear that this article falls in Item A.18.06.10 of Appendix B to the PFA Rules.
Both the analysts have applied the same standards to this product.

It is nowhere the stand of the DA vs Bal Kishan & Ors.
accused that the food article does not fall under this head or that it falls under some other head.
13. It is pertinent to note that both the chemical experts, PA and CFL, have found the presence of the synthetic colouring matter Tartrazine which is a totally prohibited item in the sample analysed.
On this point, both the reports are in conformity to each other and not at variance.
14. The defence taken by the accused no.1 is that he had purchased the dal from accused no.2 Mukesh Kumar.
In order to prove this, he examined himself as DW2and proved a bill Mark A on which the accused no.1 is relying for the purpose of benefit of warranty.
15. It would be no defence available to the accused no.1 to claim that he was not the manufacturer of the commodity in question or that he was only a retailer using the same.
A seller or packer or distributor or manufacturer would operate in different fields and all of them can be held liable in their separate areas.
Sale of adulterated food article is prohibited.
The definition of 'sale' under section 2 (xiii) is very wide which includes storing or exposing for sale as a retailer and even attempt to sell and also sale for analysis.

The only benefit which the accused can claim on this ground is under section 19(2) of PFA Act which would apply only if he is able to show that he had purchased the product against a warranty and had been selling the product in the same manner as purchased by him.

16. Even if the documents relied upon by him are accepted, that DA vs Bal Kishan & Ors.

4 would not come to his rescue.
There is nothing to connect the lifted sample of dal arhar to the dal allegedly purchased through these documents bill Mark A which is photocopy.
The dal was lifted from an open gunny bag bearing no label declaration.

Thus, there is nothing to show that the dal lifted from the shop was the same dal which the accused no.1 had allegedly purchased from accused no.2.
17.
Even otherwise, the bill produced by the accused do not qualify to give warranty to the accused under section 19(2) of the PFA Act.
For that, specific language is to be used as per Rule 12-A and as per Form-VIA, PFA Rules.

Reliance in this regard can be placed on M/s. Muralidhar Shyamlal v.
State of Assam [1996(I) PFA Cases 86].

sentences.text: There is no batch number / code number or any other means to identify the dal sold to be the one lifted.
Again, the bill/invoice should carry a warranty in the prescribed language.
Therefore, it is certain that the warranty as prescribed by Rule 12- A and Form VI-A of PFA Rules is not there on the bill.

18. Further, it is to be understood that the benefit of warranty under section 19(2) of PFA Act would be available only when there is a written warranty from the supplier/seller in addition to the fact that it has been sold in the same condition as was purchased.
Both the conditions have to be fulfilled simultaneously.
There is further no evidence to the effect that the dal was in same state or condition when sold/used.
There is no witness who could depose that the dal lifted from possession of the accused was in the same condition as was purchased though the bill in question.

DA vs Bal Kishan & Ors.
19.

The case in hand would be therefore covered under section 2(ia)
(a) of PFA Act as there is evidence to show that it was not of the nature, substance or quality which it is purported to be as per PFA Rules.
The case would fall under section 2(ia)(j) as there is presence of colour which is not permitted in this article.
Violation of section 2(ia)(j) is punishable under section 16(1A) and violation of section 2(ia)(a) is punishable under section 16(i)(a) of PFA Act.
But being graver offence, conviction can be under section 16(1A) of PFA Act.
20. Having said so, it can be said that the complainant / prosecution has been able to establish its case and prove the guilt of the accused beyond the shadow of reasonable doubt.

It has been proved that the accused had sold adulterated food in violation of section 2(ia)(a) and (j) of PFA Act read with Rules 23, 28 and 29 of PFA Rules, and has committed the offence punishable under section 7/16(1A) of PFA Act.
21.
Thus, the accused no.1 is held guilty and convicted for the offence punishable under section 16(1A) of the PFA Act and accused no. 2 is acquitted of the charges.

Let the matter be listed for arguments on sentence Announced in the open court this 26th day of July 2018 SAMAR VISHAL ACMM-II (New Delhi), PHC DA vs Bal Kishan & Ors.
Da vs Bal Kishan & Ors.
